bands.1:
In Inkwell Bay, the sun never quite sets. The sky stays purple. The water is as black as ink.

"This is the longest sunset in the world," says Tully. "Eight hundred years!"

"That's not a real fact," says Indi.

Gus sneezes, and the boat springs a leak. Tiny sparks light up all around you. The whole bay glows blue.

Everything here glows. Danglebys hang shining threads from the cliffs. A sleepy bird pretends to be a branch, until Mo sits on it.

At the end of the bay is a huge gold building. Its chimneys puff out glowing words: #HERO and #RESCUE. The sign says, "MAXX'S CONTENT FACTORY. WRITTEN BY MAXX (PROBABLY)."

"That's not on Wren's map," says Tully. Wren frowns. "It must be new."

"He has never written anything himself," says Wren.

Then white shapes float along the jetty. They have black holes for eyes.

"Ghosts!" squeaks Mo.

"Why don't ghosts tell lies?" whispers Gus. "Because you can see right through them!"

"That's MY joke," says Mo.

One ghost trips over. A pen rolls out. It is not a ghost. It is a tired man in a bedsheet. A big 7 is painted on it.

"I'm a ghostwriter," he says. "I write things for Maxx. Then Maxx says he wrote them."

He tells you everything. Fifty ghostwriters work in the factory. They write every caption and every catchphrase. Their desks are lit by glowing Creatures in jars.

"There is one room we can't go in," says Seven. "Maxx keeps a script there. We call it the Sorry Script. It's for the day he gets caught."

A whistle blows. "Ghost Seven! Back to work!"

Seven runs off. A page falls out of his sheet. It is a caption for tomorrow.

"Maxx rescues the rare Beamquid from smelly pirates in a leaky boat!"

"We're the pirates," says Zed.

Under the jetty, a little squid shines its light up at you.
bands.2:
In Inkwell Bay, the sun never quite goes down. The sky stays a deep purple, and the water stays as black as spilt ink.

"Statistically," says Tully, "this is the longest sunset in the world. Eight hundred years and counting."

"That's not a real statistic," says Indi.

"Prove it."

Gus sneezes. The boat springs a leak, the water sloshes, and suddenly Brinkles light up all around the hull. Every splash makes them brighter, until the whole bay is glowing blue.

Everything here glows. Danglebys hang shining threads from the cliffs. Asiflies blink among the trees. A Tawnip frogmouth pretends to be a branch, until Mo sits on it.

Mo's dinner is liquorice-and-lentil soup, "black, to match the bay". It tastes like a tyre.

At the end of the bay squats a huge gold building with three chimneys. Instead of smoke, they puff out glowing words: #HERO, #RESCUE, #SOBLESSED. A sign blinks over the door: "MAXX'S CONTENT FACTORY. 100% WRITTEN BY MAXX (PROBABLY)."

"That's not on Wren's map," says Tully. Wren frowns. "It must be new."

"He's never written anything himself," Wren mutters. "Not even a birthday card."

Then a line of white shapes floats along the jetty towards the factory. They have round black holes for eyes.

"Ghosts!" squeaks Mo.

"Why don't ghosts tell lies?" whispers Gus. "Because you can see right through them!"

"That's MY joke," hisses Mo.

One of the ghosts trips over its own sheet. A pen rolls out of its sleeve. It isn't a ghost at all. It's a tired young man in a bedsheet with a big 7 painted on the front.

"I'm a ghostwriter," he sighs. "I write things for Maxx, and he says he wrote them. I wrote 'Smash that heart button like it owes you money.' He never even said thank you."

Ghostwriter Seven tells you everything. Fifty ghostwriters work in the factory, writing every caption and every tearful speech. Their desks are lit by glowing Creatures in jars, because Maxx says electric lights are "bad for the vibe".

"There's one room on the top floor that we're not allowed in," says Seven. "Maxx keeps a script there, locked in a gold box. We call it the Sorry Script."

"What's it for?" asks Wren.

"For the day he gets caught."

Up at the factory, a whistle blows. "Ghost Seven! Break's over!"

Seven scrambles away, but a page flutters out of his sheet. It's tomorrow's caption.

"Maxx bravely rescues the rare Beamquid from a gang of smelly pirates in a leaky old boat!"

"Hang on," says Zed. "We're the pirates."

Under the jetty, something glows. A little squid shines its beam straight up at you.

bands.4:
In Inkwell Bay, the sun never quite goes down. It has been sinking for as long as anyone can remember without ever actually setting, so that the sky stays a deep, bruised purple and the water stays as black as spilt ink.

"Statistically," says Tully, "this is the longest sunset in the world. Eight hundred years and counting."

"That's not a real statistic," says Indi.

"Prove it."

As the Soggy Biscuit drifts in, Gus sneezes. The boat springs a leak, the water sloshes, and sparks of blue flicker to life all around the hull. They're Brinkles, specks of sea sparkle that glow brighter every time the water is stirred. One splash, then two, and within seconds the whole bay is blazing.

Everything here glows. Danglebys hang shining threads from the cliffs like strings of fairy lights. Asiflies blink on and off among the trees, and a pair of Natterflits chatter as they glide from branch to branch. On a low bough, a Tawnip frogmouth pretends to be a branch, and does a very convincing job of it, until Mo sits on it.

"Sorry!" says Mo. "Why did the frogmouth get a job? Because it was so good at looking busy!"

The Tawnip just stares at him, which is worse than any groan.

Mo's dinner is liquorice-and-lentil soup, "black, to match the bay". It tastes exactly like a tyre.

At the far end of the bay squats an enormous gold building with three tall chimneys. Instead of smoke, the chimneys puff out glowing words that drift up into the sky: #HERO, #RESCUE, #SOBLESSED. A neon sign blinks over the front door: "MAXX'S CONTENT FACTORY. 100% WRITTEN BY MAXX (PROBABLY)."

"That's not on Wren's map," says Tully. Wren frowns. "It must be new."

"He's never written anything himself," Wren mutters, so quietly that only you hear. "Not even a birthday card."

Then, as the purple sky darkens one more shade, a line of white figures floats along the jetty towards the factory. You can't see their feet. They have round black holes for eyes.

"Ghosts!" squeaks Mo, and dives behind Gus.

"Why don't ghosts tell lies?" whispers Gus. "Because you can see right through them!"

"That's MY joke," hisses Mo.

One of the ghosts stops, turns, and trips over the hem of its own sheet. It lands face first on the jetty, and a pen rolls out of its sleeve. It isn't a ghost at all. It's a tired young man in a white bedsheet with a big number 7 painted on the front.

"Please don't tell anyone you saw me fall over," he groans. "I'm a ghostwriter."

"A ghost writer?" says Zed.

"Ghostwriter. One word. I write things for Maxx, and then he says he wrote them. I wrote 'Smash that heart button like it owes you money.' He's never even said thank you."

Ghostwriter Seven tells you everything. There are fifty ghostwriters in the factory, and they write every caption, every catchphrase and every tearful speech. They wear the sheets so nobody ever sees a real person going in. Their desks are lit by glowing Creatures trapped in jars and lampshades, because Maxx says electric lights are "bad for the vibe". If a writer complains, they're fired, and every word they ever wrote is deleted.

"There's one room on the top floor that even we're not allowed in," says Seven, glancing over his shoulder. "Maxx keeps a script up there, locked in a gold box. We call it the Sorry Script."

"What's it for?" asks Wren.

"For the day he gets caught."

Up at the factory, a whistle shrieks. "Ghost Seven!" bellows a Goldie. "Break's over!"

Seven scrambles up and runs, but as he does, a page flutters out of his sheet and lands at your feet. It's tomorrow's caption, already written, waiting for a video that hasn't been filmed yet.

"Maxx bravely rescues the rare Beamquid from a gang of smelly pirates in a leaky old boat!"

Zed reads it twice. Then, slowly, he looks round at the patched sails, at Gus sniffing his own sleeve, and at the Soggy Biscuit, which is quietly leaking onto his shoes.

"Smelly pirates," he says. "Leaky old boat." He doesn't need to finish.

Under the jetty, something glows. A little squid with a lamp on its head shines its beam straight up at you, as if it already knows.
